fields.sections.2.exchanges.1.con.words: Dillahunty argues that debt, war, and historical differences cannot justify owning people, because inescapable property status destroys autonomy and leaves biblical slavery morally indefensible.
fields.sections.2.exchanges.1.con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty shifts from terminology to moral substance by contrasting ordinary work with an arrangement one cannot quit, anchoring lost autonomy in ownership, inheritance, sale, beating, war captivity, and Hagar’s forced return. Principal limitation: His movement from these concrete practices to broad claims about biblical racism, misogyny, and inequality outruns this reply’s support, while categorical language about the affirmative neglects historical differences he expressly concedes. Live burden: The argument must keep its autonomy case distinct from wider accusations and show why the cited property incidents defeat debt-repayment and prisoner-of-war defenses without relying on rhetorical shock. Locked score: The fixed score of 83 reflects direct, highly relevant engagement and a coherent exit-and-ownership test, tempered by uneven focus, limited support for sweeping claims, and insufficiently charitable characterization.
